newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Third world groups hit West over trade-labour link.
newsitem.headline: Third world groups hit West over trade-labour link.

text.p: Asia-based development groups hit out this weekend against United States-led Western efforts to force a "social clause" on to the agenda of the first Ministerial Conference of the World Trade Organisation.

At a three-day Singapore seminar on the eve of the trade ministers' gathering, they said any linkage between WTO rules and labour conditions would only worsen the situation of workers, both adults and children, in emerging economies.

"Western groups who push this issue are either misguided or simply caught up in what is in essence a protectionist effort to force up the cost of developing country products," said Martin Khor of the Malaysia-based Third World Network.

"We have seen in our country how a U.S. campaign against child labour has in fact driven young people out of jobs and on to the streets, often into prostitution," said Farhad Mazar, from a Bangladesh body working for social advance among the poor.

They were speaking as across this city the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) was calling on the trade ministers, who meet from Monday to Friday, to set up a working group on labour standards.

The United States, backed by some member countries of the European Union, has recognised the strength of the opposition and does not go so far, arguing simply for the ministers to accept that some WTO discussion on the issue is needed.

Governments of developing countries have made clear they will stoutly resist any such effort, retorting that the West is simply engaged in trying to destroy the competitive edge the cheaper labour cost of their products gives them.

But representatives of the groups at the Third World seminar made clear they stood well apart from some governments in poorer states who take an authoritarian line on labour rights and others who do not crack down on bad employers.

"We fight for better working conditions, and I have been in jail myself as a result of the struggle," said Mazar, whose organisation -- Policy Research for a Development Alternative -- focuses on the child labour issue.
"But we are realists and know what the problem really is about. Most working children in our countries have no choice but to earn money for themselves and their families.

"If they are driven out of the official factories because of international pressure, as many have been already in Bangladesh, there is almost no way we can monitor them and they are more open to exploitation than ever."

Washington pressure to end child labour in the clothing industry in Bangladesh, he argued, had been driven by the powerful U.S. lobby of textile manufacturers and unions, concerned at loss of both domestic market and industry jobs.

One paradox in the trade-and-labour debate is the strongly differing stances of Western-based non-governmental development organisations (NGOs) and those like the Third World Network based in the emerging economies.

Khor said this was largely because Western NGOs often had close ties to social democratic or labour parties, usually close to the labour unions who believe widespread unemployment in the West is due to a transfer of jobs to lower-wage economies.

Chakravarthi Raghavan, also of the Third World Network and a Geneva-based Indian authority on trade, said there was wide support in countries of the South for international pressure on their governments to behave on human rights.
But efforts to try to force them in this direction by incorporating labour rights into the trade rules of the WTO -- as openly sought by Western union groupings -- were counter-productive, he said.
